TITLE: Informative View Contribution via View-to-Instance Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We propose a new regularization term that encourages the model to learn a view-to-instance mutual information score, quantifying the amount of new information each view contains about an instance, and contribute it to the contrastive loss. This regularization is based on the idea that each view should carry some unique, informative quality about the corresponding instance. Experiments will compare standard contrastive learning to a variant with this added term, using a diverse set of real-world datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet).
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to standard SimCLR, and ablate our proposed term to understand its contribution to the overall performance. We will also compare our model to other variants that attempt to inject new similarity metrics or view-awareness, to see how mutually informative views impact performance.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our method to outperform standard contrastive learning by 1-3% in metrics such as top-1 accuracy, and reduce the gap in more distributed, low-data settings (1-5%); variations with this modification may fail to generalize and underperform SimCLR in some domains due to overfitting or conflict with current augmentation strategies.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Adaptive View Diversification for Semantic Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive view diversification mechanism that constructs novel views for each instance based on the information already captured by the model. This is achieved through a view-aware contrastive loss that updates the augmentation space at each training step to target underutilized semantic features. Specifically, we introduce a utility function that assesses the representational gain from each potential view, allowing for a dynamic allocation of resources to most informative views. We will compare our adaptive strategy to heuristic augmentation strategies commonly used in the literature, such as random cropping and color jittering.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our adaptive strategy against fixed hand-crafted views, a stronger poetic semantics baseline with example prototype behavior, as well as several variants of standard MoCo with implementative heuristic augmentations.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our adaptive strategy to improve the robustness and efficiency of contrastive learning, reducing the need for large batch sizes and diverse static augmentations, and eventually allow for smaller, lower-bound hardware inputs.

Note: To correctly balance with 50  GPU-hours Informative View Contribution in proposal 1, an approximation of two variants and several comparisons with simples standard models are maintained in proposal 2

TITLE: Understanding Dynamic View-Instance Information Flow
PROPOSAL: We will theoretically investigate the dynamic information flow between views and instances during contrastive learning. Specifically, we will analyze the emergence of semantic information under different augmentations and learning regimes. We will derive regret bounds for the adaptive view diversification strategy introduced in Proposal 2, and use these bounds to provide insights into the stability and convergence of informative view contributions (Proposal 1). These results will help in understanding the regularization mechanisms induced by our adaptive strategy and will guide further design improvements.
CONTROLS: We will analyze the theoretical aspects of view projection, instance narrative, and divergence problem in the framework of strong stochastic process or Gau proposal –and flexible linking –
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our analysis to provide a deeper understanding of the underpinnings of contrastive learning and the role of adaptive view diversification and informative view contribution. Our theory should ensure that our adaptive strategy reaches explicit measures that ensure it performs better under hardware hardware limitation setups – testing (numbered).

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Understanding Dynamic View-Instance Information Flow: Benchmarks and Inference
PROPOSAL: We will design a series of empirical experiments to evaluate the information flow dynamics between views and instances during contrastive learning. Using the real-world datasets from Proposal 1, we will compare different augmentation strategies, learning rates, and batch sizes to see how they impact the emergence of semantic information and the distribution of view-to-instance mutual information. We will also investigate how these factors influence the performance of the model on downstream tasks and how they relate to the effectiveness of our proposed adaptive view diversification mechanism.
CONTROLS: We will compare our findings to state-of-the-art baselines, including SimCLR and MoCo, as well as ablate our proposed mechanisms to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our experiments to provide insight into the dynamic information landscape of contrastive learning and the role of adaptive view diversification in promoting semantic information convergence, which should in turn improve the performance of the model on downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Efficient View Sampling for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an efficient view sampling strategy that reduces the computational cost of contrastive learning while maintaining its representational power. Our approach is based on the idea that a subset of views can be selected to represent the semantic characteristics of an instance, and that the remaining views can be discarded without significant loss of information. We will design a view selection algorithm that uses a metric learned from the model to determine which views are most informative and should be retained.
CONTROLS: We will compare our efficient sampling strategy to standard random sampling and ablate the different components of our approach to understand its contribution to the overall performance.
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our efficient sampling strategy to reduce the computational cost of contrastive learning by at least 20-30% while maintaining or improving its performance on downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Practically Scalable Contrastive Learning for Small-Batch Settings
PROPOSAL: We propose a practically scalable contrastive learning framework that can be effective in small-batch settings. Our approach combines the adaptive view diversification mechanism with efficient view sampling and informative view contribution regularization. We will design a hyperparameter-free learning rate schedule that adapts to the small-batch setting to improve training stability and efficiency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our framework to standard SimCLR and MoCo on small-batch datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32, and ablate the different components of our approach to understand their contribution to the overall performance.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our framework to outperform standard contrastive learning methods on small-batch datasets by at least 5-10% while maintaining comparable performance in large-batch settings.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Generalizing to Novel Domains and Tasks
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the ability of our contrastive learning framework to generalize to novel domains and tasks. We will fine-tune our pre-trained models on diverse datasets, such as ImageNet and CIFAR-100, and evaluate their performance on domain adaptation and transfer learning benchmarks. We will also design a novel adaptation loss that combines the informative view contribution regularization with a domain-invariant representation learning objective.
CONTROLS: We will compare our framework to state-of-the-art domain adaptation and transfer learning methods, and ablate the different components of our approach to understand their contribution to the overall performance.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our framework to achieve competitive or state-of-the-art performance on domain adaptation and transfer learning benchmarks, and demonstrate its ability to generalize to novel domains and tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Interpretability and Explainability of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will design an interpretability framework for contrastive learning that allows us to understand the learned representations and the information flow between views and instances. Our framework will use techniques such as feature importance analysis, saliency maps, and attention visualization to provide insights into the learning process. We will also investigate the use of our framework to interpret the decisions made by contrastive learning models on real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our interpretability framework to existing methods and ablate its components to understand their contribution to the overall performance.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our interpretability framework to provide significant insights into the learning process of contrastive learning models, and demonstrate its effectiveness in interpreting real-world datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Informative View Contribution via View-to-Instance Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We will refine our initial proposal for informative view contribution by integrating it with the other design components, such as adaptive view diversification, efficient view sampling, and practically scalable small-batch training. This will allow us to investigate how our approach can be used to improve the performance of contrastive learning on a range of real-world datasets and tasks. We will also compare our refined approach to state-of-the-art baselines and evaluate its effectiveness on a variety of evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: We will maintain the controls from previous proposals, including comparisons to SimCLR, MoCo, and ablations of individual components.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (in addition to the costs of previous proposals)
PREDICTION: We expect our refined approach to demonstrate improved performance on a range of real-world datasets and tasks, and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the informative view contribution phenomenon.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating View Mutual Information in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to estimate the mutual information between two views of the same instance using a neural network-based approach, and use this as a signal to guide augmentation design in contrastive learning. Specifically, we will train a neural estimator to approximate the mutual information between the original image and its augmented view, and use this information to select augmentations that maximize this mutual information.
CONTROLS: WEAK_AUG: a strong baseline that uses random cropping and color jittering as augmentations
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: If augmentation design is guided by view mutual information, we expect to see improved representation quality and better generalization, especially on small batches. However, this may come at the cost of slower convergence, as the model needs to spend more time exploring the augmentation space. This could fail if the mutual information estimator is noisy or biased.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Expansion for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the view mutual information approach from experiment 1 by incorporating a self-attention mechanism that adapts the view expansion in response to the model's predictions. Specifically, when the model is uncertain about the relationship between the original image and its augmented view, we expand the view space by adding more augmentations, and when it is confident, we reduce the number of augmentations to avoid over-expansion.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENT 1 (View Mutual Information), FIXED_AUG: a baseline that fixes the number of augmentations throughout training
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved representation quality and more efficient use of computational resources, especially in small-batch settings. However, this may also increase the risk of over-expansion and invalid augmentations if not properly controlled. This could fail if the self-attention mechanism is overly aggressive or conservative.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Informative Set Cover: A Criterion for Augmentation Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a principled criterion for augmentation selection that takes into account the complexity of the underlying data distribution. Specifically, we introduce a new concept called "informative set cover," which seeks to identify the smallest set of augmentations that cover the most informative regions of the data distribution. We will demonstrate how to use this criterion to select augmentations that are both informative and diverse.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-2 (View Mut. Info. and Adaptive View Expansion), RANDOM_AUG: a baseline that randomly selects augmentations
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved representation quality and faster convergence due to the more effective selection of augmentations. However, this may also lead to over-specialization if the criterion is overly optimistic about the informativeness of a particular augmentation. This could fail if the data distribution is highly non-stationary or has complex privilege structures.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining Informative Set Cover using Dynamic Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We refine the informative set cover criterion by incorporating a dynamic graph neural network (DGN) that learns to adapt to the evolving representation of the data distribution during training. Specifically, we use the DGN to update the informative set cover criterion at each iteration, taking into account the new representation generated by the contrastive learning model.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-3 (View Mut. Info., Adaptive View Expansion, and baseline for Informative Set Cover), RANDOM_AUG: a revised baseline that uses a fixed, pseudo-random set of augmentations
COST: 400 GPU-hours (additional to experiment 3's 300)
PREDICTION: We expect to see further improvements in representation quality and convergence speed, thanks to the dynamic adaptation of the informative set cover criterion. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational overhead, especially in high-dimensional data spaces. This could fail if the DGN is overly complex or unstable, leading to non-convergence of the adaptation process.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining Informative Set Cover using Dynamic Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We revise experiment 3 by refining the Informative Set Cover criterion using a dynamic graph neural network (DGN) that learns to adapt to the evolving representation of the data distribution during training. This adaptation will occur in real-time, allowing for the model to adapt to new and changing patterns in the data. Specifically, we will use the DGN to update the informative set cover criterion at each iteration, taking into account the new representation generated by the contrastive learning model.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENT 1 (View Mut. Info.), EXPERIMENT 2 (Adaptive View Expansion), FIXED_AUG: a baseline that fixes the number of augmentations throughout training
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see further improvements in representation quality and convergence speed, thanks to the dynamic adaptation of the informative set cover criterion. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational overhead, especially in high-dimensional data spaces. This could fail if the DGN is overly complex or unstable, leading to non-convergence of the adaptation process.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 3. Informative Set Cover: A Criterion for Augmentation Selection
PROPOSAL: We refine experiment 3 by exploring different variants of the informative set cover criterion and comparing their performance. Specifically, we will investigate a greedy variant, a top-k variant, and a probability-based variant, and compare their accuracy, efficiency, and convergence properties. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of the informative set cover criterion.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-2 (View Mut. Info. and Adaptive View Expansion), RANDOM_AUG: a baseline that randomly selects augmentations
COST: 250 GPU-hours (this is a revision to the original 300 GPU-hours in experiment 3)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that different variants of the informative set cover criterion may have different strengths and weaknesses, and that understanding these trade-offs will be crucial for developing more effective augmentation strategies. This could fail if the variants are not properly evaluated or compared.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation Selection via Neural Network-based Active Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a neural network-based active learning approach to select augmentations for contrastive learning. Specifically, we will use a disk-based strategy to select the most informative augmentations, where the neural network evaluates the potential informativeness of each augmentation and recommends the top-N augmentations to be selected. We will compare this approach to random augmentation selection and the informative set cover criterion.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-3 (View Mut. Info., Adaptive View Expansion, and two variants of Informative Set Cover), FIXED_AUG: a baseline that fixes the number of augmentations throughout training
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved representation quality and faster convergence due to the more informed selection of augmentations. However, this may also lead to over-fitting if the active learning approach is too aggressive, and the model becomes over-reliant on a small set of highly informative augmentations. This could fail if the neural network fails to properly evaluate the informativeness of the augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Information Flow in Contrastive Learning through Information-theoretic Quantities
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze the information flow in contrastive learning through information-theoretic quantities, such as mutual information and conditional entropy, and to investigate how different augmentation strategies and selection mechanisms affect the flow of information between the input and the output of the model. We will use theoretical analysis and experimental validation to understand the relationship between information flow and representation quality.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-4 (View Mut. Info., Adaptive View Expansion, Informative Set Cover, and Neural Network-based Active Learning), FIXED_AUG: a baseline that fixes the number of augmentations throughout training
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to gain insights into the information-theoretic mechanisms underlying contrastive learning and to develop a deeper understanding of how augmentation strategies and selection mechanisms affect the representation quality of the model. However, this may also require the development of new theoretical tools and techniques for analyzing information flow in complex neural networks. This could fail if the analysis is overly simplistic or fails to capture the complexity of the information flow.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentation Scheduling
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an adaptive augmentation scheduling technique that adjusts the number of augmentations and the frequency of augmentation updates based on the model's performance and the data distribution. This will allow the model to dynamically allocate computation resources to the most informative augmentations and to adapt to changing data distributions. We will evaluate the proposed scheduling technique on a range of contrastive learning tasks and compare its performance to existing approaches.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-5 (View Mut. Info., Adaptive View Expansion, Informative Set Cover, Neural Network-based Active Learning, and Analysis of Information Flow), FIXED_AUG: a baseline that fixes the number of augmentations throughout training
COST: 550 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved representation quality and faster convergence due to the adaptive allocation of computation resources and the continuous adaptation to changing data distributions. However, this may also require the development of effective heuristics for adaptive scheduling and tuning. This could fail if the scheduling heuristic is overly simplistic or fails to capture the complexity of the data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Contrastive Learning Methods
PROPOSAL: We propose to conduct a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of the contrastive learning methods proposed in this research, including the informativeness of view mutual information, the adaptive augmentation strategies, and the adaptive augmentation scheduling techniques. We will evaluate the performance of these methods on a range of benchmark datasets and tasks, and compare their performance to state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods.
CONTROLS: EXPERIMENTS 1-6 (all previous experiments), STATE_OF_THE_ART: a baseline that represents the current state-of-the-art in contrastive learning
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed contrastive learning methods, and to contribute to the development of more effective and robust contrastive learning approaches. This could fail if the evaluation is incomplete or biased, or if the comparison to state-of-the-art methods is not fair or thorough.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing Information Gain through Augmentations in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Experiment the viability of information-theoretic metrics (e.g. Kolmogorov complexity, conditional entropy) to quantify the information gained by augmentations, compare these metrics to the performance benefit of different augmentation strategies on a set of benchmarking datasets (e.g. CIFAR-10, ImageNet). Use established contrastive learning frameworks (e.g. SimCLR) and their adaptive variants (e.g. VICReg) to study how well these metrics correlate with augmentative benefits, thus identifying principled measures for augmentation design.
CONTROLS: Baseline: NA (experiment to establish a link between augmentation quality and information-theoretic metrics); Alternative approach: traditional hand-tuned augmentations (static/baseline).
COST: 45 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results offer initial encouragement on the use of information-theory-inspired metrics, specifically their capacity to notably differentiate well-formed from poorly performing augmentation pipelines. However, it is predicted that results might fail in cases where high-quality augmentations exist but similarly yield low information gain due to highly similar reproducing kernels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Dynamic Representational Capacity Expansion in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for self-aware, adaptive contrastive learning frameworks that dynamically modify the representational capacity for each instance based on the geometry of the data in the embedding space. Employ an infosphere-like mechanism, where each instance is given a secondary, learnable "representational handle" that changes in response to changes in the learned representations. Adversarial testing (e.g., inversion attacks) and contrastive learning objectives can then be tailored to quantify this adaptive capacity. Use the same benchmark datasets as proposal 1, alongside the DCTB dataset, for a broader exploration of representational capacity expansion.
CONTROLS: Baseline: static augmentations with fixed metrics (similarity, uniformity); Alternative approach: global, non-instance-specific capacity adjustments (e.g., perturbation-based modified JSD).
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that the novel approach shows significant adaptability of learned representations and higher intelligibility of the self-aware mechanism, however this could collapse in situation where DCTB allows adversarial transformations more room to structure, inherently piling noise on to the process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Augmentation Seed Network (AASN)
PROPOSAL: Experiment with developing an AASN, a neural network that learns to generate adaptive augmentation seeds at the beginning of each training iteration, rather than relying on fixed pre-defined augmentation strategies. This approach combines ideas from dynamic data augmentation and self-modulation in contrastive learning. Train and evaluate the AASN on multiple benchmark datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet) and compare its performance to static augmentation strategies and adaptive variants (e.g., VICReg).
CONTROLS: Baseline: NA (experiment to establish the effectiveness of the AASN); Alternative approach: human-engineered augmentations (static).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that AASN shows significant performance improvements due to its ability to adapt to the changing data distribution, particularly when the learning dynamics are volatile or not well-captured by the hand-designed augmentations. However, results might fail in cases where extreme outliers or distributional shifts impede learning from past augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inferring Augmentation Effectiveness through Visual Attention-based Analysis
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of visual attention-based analysis to infer the effectiveness of augmentations in contrastive learning. Train a visual attention model (e.g., ResNet + Att mechanisms) to focus on the most informative regions of the data when evaluating the effectiveness of different augmentations (e.g., rotation, color jittering). Evaluate the model on multiple benchmark datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet) and compare its performance to existing methods (e.g., AUROC, PR-AUC) of assessing augmentation effectiveness.
CONTROLS: Baseline: traditional methods for augmentation effectiveness assessment; Alternative approach: random sampling of augmentations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that the visual attention-based analysis shows higher accuracy in inferring augmentation effectiveness, particularly when the data distribution is complex or when augmentations are designed to capture subtle features. However, results might fail in cases where the visual attention model struggles to capture global features or when augmentations cause significant data decomposition.

PROPOSAL: Analyze the vulnerability of contrastive learning to augmentation noise by introducing controlled noise perturbations to augmentations (e.g., Gaussian noise, out-of-distribution data) and studying their impact on model performance, information gain, and representational capacity expansion. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distillation of Adaptive Augmentation Strategies for Scalable Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a distillation framework that coherently extracts the most critical adaptive augmentation strategies from multiple experiments, models, and datasets. This framework will combine insights from information gain, representational capacity expansion, and augmentation noise vulnerability to identify a compact set of key augmentations that consistently improve contrastive learning under different conditions. Evaluate the distilled augmentation set across various benchmark datasets and analyze its ability to generalize to new, unseen settings.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a manually curated set of augmentations; Alternative approach: a randomly sampled set of augmentations.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that the distillation framework effectively identifies a small set of augmentations that boosts contrastive learning performance across a range of settings. However, it is predicted that the distilled set might perform poorly in very unusual or adversarial scenarios, where the original adaptive strategies fail to generalize.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Black-Box Optimization Meets Contrastive Learning: Efficient Augmentation Strategy Search
PROPOSAL: Utilize black-box optimization algorithms (e.g., Bayesian optimization, evolution strategies) to search for effective augmentation strategies for contrastive learning tasks. This involves formulating the problem as a maximization of a proxy objective, such as the validation accuracy of a contrastive model, and using a black-box optimization algorithm to efficiently search for optimal augmentation strategies. Evaluate the performance of the black-box optimized augmentation strategies on various benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a set of predefined augmentations; Alternative approach: random search.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that black-box optimization can effectively find augmentation strategies that outperform the baseline and alternative approaches. However, it is predicted that the optimization process may converge to an overfitting solution if the proxy objective is too optimistic or if the search space is too complex, resulting in a non-generalizable solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation on Transfer Learning and Adaptation with Optimal Augmentation Strategies
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability and adaptability of contrastive models trained with optimal augmentation strategies (found through the methods in the previous proposals). Evaluate the performance of these models on downstream tasks, such as object detection, segmentation, and classification, with varying degrees of adaptation (e.g., using a new dataset, modifying the input space). Compare the performance of models trained with optimal augmentation strategies to those trained with traditional random or fixed augmentation strategies.
CONTROLS: Baseline: models trained with traditional random or fixed augmentation strategies; Alternative approach: models fine-tuned on the new dataset.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The expectation is that models trained with optimal augmentation strategies exhibit better transferability and adaptability on downstream tasks. However, it is predicted that overfitting to the new dataset may occur if the optimal augmentation strategies are too specific to the original dataset, and therefore the model's performance might degrade in the presence of new adversarial or unseen data.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Measuring Information Gain through Instance-Specific Views
